title: Thought and deed
hook: his legacy joins philosophy and law

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: resting in tiberias. A tomb by the Sea of Galilee, candles, small stones, and a name said with a blessing. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

Two books on one shelf. One is thick with rules: how to pray, how to give, how to keep Shabbat, how a court works, what to eat. The other is full of questions: what words about God can mean, why the commandments exist, how a mind draws near to God. The same man wrote both. A reader could treat them as two different authors, the lawyer and the philosopher. But look at how each one begins and ends, and the two start to reach for each other. Today's word is the bridge between them.
screen: `A BOOK OF RULES.` → `A BOOK OF QUESTIONS.` → `ONE AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: Thought and deed. Turn it four ways. First, the code starts with thought. Before a single rule about food or Shabbat, the Mishneh Torah opens with knowing that there is a first Being, and with love and awe of God. The law book stands on a foundation of thinking. Second, the Guide ends with deed. You heard it last week: the book of philosophy closes with Jeremiah, and with going out to do kindness, justice and righteousness. The thinking book lands on doing. Third, an old argument. The Talmud tells of sages gathered in an upper room in Lod, asking which is greater, study or deed. Rabbi Tarfon said deed. Rabbi Akiva said study. And they all answered together: study is greater, because study leads to deed. Notice the answer. Study wins by pointing past itself. Fourth, the other side of the scale. In Pirkei Avot, Shimon, the son of Rabban Gamliel, says that study isn't the main thing; the deed is. Read together, the two sayings hold each other in place. Thought without deed goes nowhere. Deed without thought can go anywhere. This is the shape of Maimonides' legacy. The philosopher wrote law, and the lawgiver wrote philosophy, and each was meant to lead into the other. And it's the shape of this week: an argument in the margin, a rival reading, a son's prayer, an honest page, a prayer's true label, a grave by the water. Each one was a thought someone carried out into the world.
screen: `THE CODE STARTS WITH THOUGHT.` · `THE GUIDE ENDS WITH DEED.` · `STUDY LEADS TO DEED.` · `THE DEED IS THE MAIN THING.` · then, large: `THOUGHT AND DEED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Choose one idea from this week that stayed with you. Credit before criticism. A second reader. Saying a line slowly. An honest label. A teacher's name. Hold it for a few breaths. Now give it a pair of hands: one small act, today, that this thought would actually do. Name the time and place. Let the thought and the act sit together, joined. The bell holds the time.
Thought and deed. Maimonides' legacy: law that begins with knowing God, and philosophy that ends in kindness, each leading into the other. Today's word.
Your line: thought and deed. Today, do the act you joined to your thought, and notice how the thinking changes once it's done. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.
